## Active

### D-700 — blong-agent: an engine is a framework adapter in blong-gogo

> _2026-10-31 · realm/blong-agent · active_

The SDK client belongs to a base adapter in core/blong-gogo, src/adapter/server/agent.ts, because a
handler may not drive an SDK of its own. Four engine kinds sit behind that one adapter: Vercel AI
SDK, Mastra, DeepSeek Harness and a scripted sim. DeepSeek is driven through the published
@deepseek-ai/dsh-sdk-client, which spawns the dsh runtime over stdio JSON-RPC; the clone at
work/blong/deepseek-harness is the reference for its API and not a vendored dependency. The sim
replays a scripted dialogue so the tests need no network and no key. The harness is alpha and its
client a release candidate, so each kind is imported dynamically and a missing package fails one
account rather than the process. The methods stay three segments on the adapter's own namespace:
engine.step.run, engine.session.run, engine.session.close and engine.account.check.

### D-702 — blong-agent: a late answer is a database row, not a promise

> _2026-10-31 · realm/blong-agent · active_

The hot path is blong-chat's parked promise, awaited with a thirty minute timeout passed as
timeoutMs. An answer that arrives after that promise is gone, or on a pod that does not hold the
workspace, must be forwarded by blong-chat to agent.answer.receive, which writes an agent_answer row
keyed by the prompt id. The worker that owns the session consumes the row and resumes from the
checkpoint, and a repeated delivery is idempotent on the prompt id. A broker may also wake that
worker the moment the row lands, but the row is the record and the tick poll is the fallback
(@@D-709). This needs one change in realm/blong-chat: an answer nobody is waiting for must honour
the configured forward instead of being acknowledged and dropped.

### D-704 — blong-agent: the worker is a group on the dispatch orchestrator

> _2026-10-31 · realm/blong-agent · active_

The background loop hangs off the realm's own dispatch orchestrator, orchestrator/agentDispatch.ts:
a worker group exposes agent.worker.tick, and the orchestrator's start opens an unref'd interval
behind an in-flight guard while stop clears it. Keeping the worker on the same orchestrator as the
methods it calls is what lets the loop reach them without a broker, and exposing the cycle as a
method is what lets a test drive exactly one claim and run without waiting on a timer. A cron
schedule cannot hold the awaiting call the hot path needs, and it cannot stop a second pass from
overlapping the first.

### D-705 — blong-agent: a recovered session asks the channel before it writes

> _2026-10-31 · realm/blong-agent · active_

A boot janitor scans only the workspace directory of its own host and matches it against sessions
whose lease has expired. A match is not resumed silently: the channel is asked to confirm, because a
crash may have interrupted a write. Confirmation resumes from the latest checkpoint, a refusal
purges the directory and fails the ticket, and no answer leaves the session suspended for the next
boot rather than destroying work nobody judged. The same confirmation covers a repeat ticket, so a
resumed session states what it is about to do before it edits anything.

### D-706 — blong-agent: the realm is realm/blong-agent, the blueprint is core

> _2026-10-31 · realm/blong-agent · active_

Two folders would otherwise share the name. core/blong-agent is an evaluation blueprint with no
package manifest, and the new realm is the package feasibleone blong-agent under realm/blong-agent.
The blueprint is worth adopting as a test inside the realm later, because it is the only measure of
how well the instructions produce a realm, and that adoption is explicitly out of scope for this
plan. Until someone does it, a path beginning with core/blong-agent means the blueprint and never
the realm.

### D-707 — blong-agent: the ticket is an adapter; fixtures now, blong-task later

> _2026-10-31 · realm/blong-agent · active_

The pool belongs to a realm that does not exist yet: blong-task will own tickets, claim and lease,
so blong-agent holds no agent_ticket table. The agent reaches the pool through a task adapter whose
first implementation is a fixture list in the realm, seeded from YAML, exposing nextClaim, release
and edit; the worker's ownership rule lives on the agent's own session row, which records the worker
that holds the workspace. When blong-task lands it replaces that one adapter's implementation, and
the loop does not change.

### D-708 — blong-agent: a session names its engine mode, step or native loop

> _2026-10-31 · realm/blong-agent · active_

DeepSeek Harness runs its own agent loop; the SDK client spawns the dsh runtime and a prompt returns
when the whole agent is idle. An adapter that insisted on one turn would fight that, so a session
records its mode: step, where the realm owns the loop and the adapter returns tool calls, or native,
where the engine owns the loop and reports its events. Both write the neutral transcript to a
checkpoint, and a native session also stores the engine session id, which is what resumeSession
needs after a restart. Vercel, Mastra and the simulator are step engines; DeepSeek is native.

### D-709 — blong-agent: a broker wakes the owner, the answer row is the truth

> _2026-10-31 · realm/blong-agent · active_

A broker is a wake-up, never the record: the answer is a row first, and a notification carrying the
session and prompt id tells the owning pod to look now instead of on its next tick. The notify
adapter has a redis implementation and a kafka one, chosen by configuration, kafka using a unique
consumer group per pod so every pod sees every message, and the tick poll remains the fallback that
makes a lost notification harmless. This keeps correctness in the database and latency in the
broker.

### D-710 — blong-agent: the agent may run commands; the container is the boundary

> _2026-10-31 · realm/blong-agent · active_

The agent runs commands in its workspace, because a coding agent that cannot build or test is not
one. The boundary is the container rather than a command allowlist: execFile with an argv array and
no shell, the ticket directory as cwd, a wall-clock timeout, an output cap, a scrubbed environment
that carries no secrets, and one event row per command. The capability is switchable per deployment,
and the deployment runs it on a pod that mounts only the workspace volume.

### D-711 — blong-agent: a native engine brings its own tools, the realm brings the human

> _2026-10-31 · realm/blong-agent · active_

DeepSeek Harness ships fs, shell and sandbox tools and runs them itself, so a native session already
reads, writes and runs commands with the ticket directory as its root; the harness enforces the
boundary the workspace adapter enforces for a step engine. Registering the realm's own tools with it
would mean serving MCP from the realm, a second protocol with no new capability, so that is a later
decision. What the realm must supply is the human: the client's onUserQuestion answers an ask and
onRequest handles an approval request, and both route to the same question handler the step path
uses. A native account therefore differs from a step account in who owns the tool loop and which
tools run, not in how a person is asked.

### D-712 — blong-agent: an adapter owns its namespace and may be instanced twice

> _2026-10-31 · realm/blong-agent · active_

An adapter instance owns its namespace, and one base adapter may be instantiated more than once in a
process, which is what chat already does with slack and viber both extending adapter.webhook.
Methods are therefore named after the namespace and not after the realm: engine.step.run belongs to
the engine instance of adapter.agent, and a second instance named review answers review.step.run
with its own account map. The consequence for this realm is that a session must record the instance
it ran on as well as the account inside it, because the same alias may exist in both and a resume
that guessed the wrong instance would reach the wrong endpoint.

### D-717 — A k8s contribution belongs in the default activation block, not release

> _2026-10-31 · realm/blong-agent · active_

A k8s tree is generated by a k8s run, which merges the default block and nothing else, so a
contribution declared under release is invisible to the generator and the tree comes out without the
volume, the Secret reference or the sizing. The division that works is: the k8s keys live in
default, where only the generator reads them, and anything that must differ between a checkout and a
deployment (the workspace root, which names the directory a claim is mounted at) lives in release,
where the deployment's value belongs. A realm that puts both in release gets a tree that silently
lacks its resources; one that puts both in default gets a checkout writing to a cluster path.

## Superseded

### D-699 — blong-agent: the engine port is one model turn, not one agent run

> _2026-10-31 · realm/blong-agent · superseded_

Adapters implement a single model turn: they receive the neutral transcript and the tool definitions
and return assistant text and tool calls, executing nothing themselves. The realm owns the loop, so
the transcript it checkpoints is engine-neutral and a session can change engine, or resume on
another host, by replaying that transcript. This is the only shape that makes DeepSeek Harness
resumable, because a Cordis context lives in RAM and cannot be serialised. The cost is that every
turn re-sends the transcript, and a runaway loop is bounded by an explicit step limit rather than by
the SDK.

the one-turn contract is the step mode; a native engine keeps its own loop

Superseded by `D-708`.

### D-701 — blong-agent: the realm owns the ticket pool and leases it in the database

> _2026-10-31 · realm/blong-agent · superseded_

Tickets are rows in agent_ticket, claimed with one conditional update that sets workerId and
leaseExpiresAt, so two workers cannot take the same ticket and a dead worker's lease expires on its
own. A claim is refused when the ticket names a workspace that does not exist on this host, because
the only process that may touch those files is the one holding the volume. No broker is involved in
the first pass: the database is both the pool and the lease record.

the pool is blong-task's; agent reaches it through a fixture task port

Superseded by `D-707`.

### D-703 — blong-agent: the workspace is a per-ticket git-rollback directory

> _2026-10-31 · realm/blong-agent · superseded_

A ticket gets workspaceRoot slash ticketId, created from a configured template and recorded with the
base commit it started from. Every tool resolves its path inside that directory and refuses an
escape, because a model writing a parent path is the ordinary case rather than the attack. Rollback
is git checkout plus git clean inside that directory, and the agent executes no shell command in the
first pass: a build or test tool is a later capability that needs its own decision.

the shell is allowed inside the container boundary

Superseded by `D-710`.
